f: Statute vs administrative rule: what is the difference, with one Florida real estate example of each?
b: A statute is passed by the Legislature (Chapter 475 F.S., the license law). A rule is adopted by an agency under a statute's authority (Rule 61J2 F.A.C., e.g., escrow deposit deadlines adopted by FREC).

f: DBPR vs FREC — who investigates, who disciplines, who issues licenses?
b: DBPR issues licenses and investigates complaints. FREC adopts rules and disciplines (final orders). Courts handle crimes and civil damages.

f: The three elements that require a real estate license.
b: A real estate service, for another, for compensation (paid, promised or expected).

f: A builder's salaried employee sells the builder's homes. Then she's paid per closing. License needed?
b: Salaried only: exempt. Paid per closing: license required — the exemption depends on no commission/transaction-based pay.

f: Mutual recognition: who can use it, and what exam do they take?
b: Only applicants who are NOT Florida residents when they apply, licensed in a state with an agreement. They take a 40-question Florida law exam and need 30 correct.

f: Missed post-license education vs missed continuing education: consequences?
b: Post-license (45 hrs) missed before first renewal → license null and void. CE (14 hrs) missed at a later renewal → involuntary inactive (recoverable for 2 years).

f: Involuntary inactive for 18 months. What does reactivation require?
b: The 28-hour commission-prescribed reactivation course (more than 12 but less than 24 months). ≤12 months: 14 hours. >24 months: license expired.

f: What event starts a 10-day clock and what event starts a 30-day clock for a licensee's duty to notify DBPR?
b: 10 days: change of mailing or e-mail address (also a change of employing broker). 30 days: conviction, finding of guilt, or guilty or nolo contendere plea to any crime.
Group license: a sales associate (or broker associate) works for several CONNECTED entities of one owner-developer. Multiple licenses: a BROKER holds separate licenses for unconnected brokerages.
Transaction broker (unless single agent or no brokerage relationship is established in writing).

f: Name the four duties owed ONLY by a single agent.
b: Loyalty, obedience, (full) confidentiality, full disclosure.

f: Transaction-broker duty not to reveal that the seller will take less, the buyer will pay more, a party's motivation, or facts a party asks to keep confidential.
b: Limited confidentiality.

f: When must the No Brokerage Relationship Notice be given?
b: Before showing the property.

f: When must the Single Agent Notice be given?
b: Before or at the time of entering into a listing or representation agreement, or before showing property — whichever comes first.

f: List four situations where brokerage disclosure is NOT required.
b: Any four of: party already represented; bona fide open house/model showing; unanticipated casual encounter; general factual questions about advertised property; general info about qualifications/firm; auctions; appraisals; leases without an option to buy ≤4 units; nonresidential/commercial; business enterprises (except ≤4 residential units).

f: Latent defect vs stigma: which must be disclosed in Florida?
b: Known latent material defects (hidden roof leak, flooding) must be disclosed. Death on the property and HIV/AIDS status are declared not material.

f: Which duties survive termination of a brokerage relationship?
b: Confidentiality and accounting for funds.

f: Deposit received Wednesday (no holidays). Associate's deadline? Broker's deadline?
b: Associate → broker: end of Thursday (next business day). Broker deposits: end of Monday (Thu 1, Fri 2, Mon 3).
Commingling: mixing personal and escrow funds. Conversion: using escrow funds for personal or unauthorized purposes (more serious).
Mediation (all consent, 90 days), Arbitration (all consent, binding), Litigation (interpleader), Escrow disbursement order from FREC (only if the broker holds the funds).

f: Two statutory situations where a broker may return a deposit to the buyer without notifying FREC.
b: A residential condo buyer cancels under s. 718.503; the buyer in good faith fails to satisfy the contract's financing clause.

f: An ad by a licensee that omits the registered brokerage name.
b: Blind ad.

f: Who may pay a sales associate for real estate services?
b: Only the sales associate's employing broker (or owner-developer employer).

f: Put in order: final order, probable cause, investigation, formal complaint, hearing, complaint, appeal.
b: Complaint → investigation → probable cause → formal complaint → hearing → final order → appeal (30 days).
Misrepresentation: a false statement (or concealment) of material fact. Culpable negligence: reckless indifference to others' rights — beyond simple carelessness, without intent to deceive.

f: Who cannot recover from the Real Estate Recovery Fund?
b: A licensee who acted as a licensee in the transaction (e.g., commission disputes); also excluded: amounts above caps, treble damages, court costs, attorney's fees, interest.

Steering: guiding buyers toward/away from areas by protected class. Blockbusting: scaring owners into selling because a protected class is moving in. Redlining: lender refusing or varying loans by area.
Modification: physical change to the unit (usually tenant pays). Accommodation: change in rules/policies (e.g., service animal despite no-pets rule).

f: TILA's 3-business-day right of rescission applies to which loans?
b: Refinances and home-equity loans on the borrower's principal residence — not purchase loans, not investment property.

f: Match: housing / credit / public accommodations / lending data.
b: Fair Housing Act / ECOA / ADA / HMDA.

f: Security deposit timeline after the tenant moves out.
b: 15 days to return if no claim; certified-mail notice of claim within 30 days; tenant has 15 days to object. Missing the 30-day notice forfeits the claim.
Remainder: future interest goes to a third party (remainderman). Reversion: it returns to the grantor or heirs.

Assignment: the ENTIRE remaining term; assignee pays landlord; original tenant secondarily liable unless released. Sublease: part of the term or space; subtenant pays tenant; tenant stays primarily liable.

f: Married couple, deed silent. Unmarried pair, deed silent. How is title held in each case?
b: Married: tenancy by the entireties. Unmarried: tenancy in common.

f: Florida homestead: name the three separate legal effects.
b: (1) Protection from forced sale by most creditors; (2) restrictions on transfer and devise when there is a spouse/minor child (spouse joins deeds and mortgages); (3) property-tax exemption.
Condo: deed to a unit (real property) + undivided share of common elements. Co-op: shares in the corporation + proprietary lease (personal property).

f: General warranty vs special warranty deed.
b: General: grantor warrants against defects from any time. Special: only defects arising during the grantor's ownership.

f: What makes a Florida deed valid, and what is needed only for recording?
b: Valid: writing, competent grantor, identifiable grantee, consideration, words of conveyance, legal description, grantor's signature + 2 witnesses, delivery and acceptance. Recording: notary acknowledgment.

f: Easement appurtenant vs easement in gross.
b: Appurtenant: benefits an adjacent parcel (dominant/servient), runs with the land. In gross: benefits a person or company (utility), no dominant estate.

f: Adverse possession vs easement by prescription (Florida periods).
b: Adverse possession (title): 7 years + color of title or payment of taxes. Prescription (easement): 20 years of adverse use.
Accretion: gradual deposit of soil — owner gains land, boundary moves. Avulsion: sudden change — boundary does not move.

f: Four tests for whether an item is a fixture.
b: Intent (most important), method of annexation, adaptation to the property, relationship of the parties. Trade fixtures stay the tenant's.
640 ÷ (product of the denominators). Use AND to add separate parcels.

f: Where is section 1, section 6, section 31, section 36?
b: 1 = NE corner; 6 = NW; 31 = SW; 36 = SE (serpentine numbering from the NE).
Part = Total × Rate; Total = Part ÷ Rate; Rate = Part ÷ Total.
(New − Old) ÷ Old. The base is always the starting value.

f: Sale price needed to net the seller a given amount.
b: Price = (Net + fixed costs) ÷ (1 − commission rate). Never multiply the net by (1 + rate).

f: Recover the original cost from a sale price and profit %.
b: Cost = Sale ÷ (1 + profit%). For a loss: Cost = Sale ÷ (1 − loss%).
LTV = loan ÷ lesser of sale price or appraised value.

f: First month's interest on an amortized loan.
b: Balance × annual rate ÷ 12. Principal = payment − interest.

f: Deed stamps, note stamps, intangible tax — formulas and who customarily pays.
b: Deed: round price UP to $100 → ÷100 × $0.70 (seller). Note: round loan UP → ÷100 × $0.35 (buyer; new and assumed). Intangible: new loan × 0.002 (buyer).

f: Proration of unpaid property taxes: which party is debited?
b: Debit seller, credit buyer (taxes paid in arrears).

f: Proration of rent collected in advance by the seller: which party is credited?
b: Credit buyer, debit seller, for the buyer's days (including the closing day).

f: Single or double entry? Binder deposit; new mortgage; assumed mortgage; seller's payoff.
b: Deposit: credit buyer (single). New mortgage: credit buyer (single). Assumed mortgage: debit seller + credit buyer (double). Payoff: debit seller (single).

f: Housing ratio and total obligations ratio.
b: Housing = PITI ÷ gross monthly income. Total = (PITI + recurring debts) ÷ gross monthly income. Course benchmarks: 28/36 conventional; 31/43 FHA.

f: IRV and how to build NOI.
b: Value = NOI ÷ cap rate. NOI = PGI − vacancy & collection loss − operating expenses (NOT debt service or depreciation).
GRM = price ÷ MONTHLY gross rent (1–4 units). GIM = price ÷ ANNUAL gross income.
Value = land value + (cost new − accrued depreciation).
Adjust the comparable, never the subject. Comparable better → subtract; comparable inferior → add (CBS / CIA).
School tax = (assessed − 25,000) × school mills ÷ 1,000. Non-school = (assessed − 50,000*) × other mills ÷ 1,000. (*second exemption is up to $25,000, CPI-indexed since 2025.)
Cash flow = NOI − debt service. Cap rate = NOI ÷ price.
Assumption: buyer becomes personally liable (seller stays secondarily liable unless novation). Subject to: buyer pays but has no personal liability.

f: FHA vs VA: role and borrower charge.
b: FHA insures (borrower pays MIP). VA guarantees (borrower pays funding fee). Neither lends.
Primary: originates loans (banks, credit unions, mortgage bankers/brokers). Secondary: buys existing loans (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac; Ginnie Mae guarantees FHA/VA securities).
Void: no contract at all. Voidable: one party may cancel (minor, fraud, duress). Unenforceable: valid but a court won't enforce (no required writing, time-barred).

f: Exclusive right of sale vs exclusive agency: owner sells to her neighbour herself.
b: Exclusive right of sale: commission owed. Exclusive agency: no commission.

f: Effect of a counteroffer on the original offer.
b: It rejects and terminates the original offer permanently.
Variance: deviation from a dimensional rule due to hardship unique to the parcel. Special exception: a use the code allows with case-by-case approval.
Police power: regulation (zoning, codes), no compensation. Eminent domain: taking for public use, just compensation required.
1031: investment/business real property exchanged for like-kind; gain deferred; boot taxable. Residence: exclude $250k/$500k gain if owned and used 2 of last 5 years.

f: Pre-license course (sales associate) — state the exact rule.
b:
63 hours (50-minute hours), including the end-of-course exam
Conditions: The course completion becomes invalid if the state exam is not PASSED within 2 years after completing the course (V-31).
Qualifications: Mutual-recognition nonresidents skip the course (see N-007).

f: Applicant minimum age / education — state the exact rule.
b:
18 years old; high school diploma or equivalent; U.S. Social Security number
Qualifications: U.S. citizenship and Florida residency are NOT required. Florida Bar members are exempt from the pre-license course (V-31).

f: State exam passing score — state the exact rule.
b:
75 correct out of 100 (75%)
Qualifications: Mutual recognition law exam: 30 of 40 (N-007).

f: Exam time limit — state the exact rule.
b: 3.5 hours

f: Application validity — state the exact rule.
b: Expires 2 years after DBPR receives it if the applicant has not passed the exam

f: Reapplying after denial for dishonesty — state the exact rule.
b: May reapply after 2 years (manual statement)

f: Mutual recognition law exam — state the exact rule.
b:
40 questions; 30 correct to pass (75%)
Conditions: Must hold an active license in good standing in that state.
Qualifications: Florida residents cannot use mutual recognition. The other state's license must have been earned by its own course and exam. Current states (9): AL, AR, CT, GA, KY, MS, NE, RI, WV; Illinois ended Dec 31, 2025 (V-22).

f: Post-license education (sales associate) — state the exact rule.
b:
45 hours, completed before the FIRST renewal
Qualifications: Missing it makes the license NULL AND VOID; must requalify (63-hour course and state exam). Exempt: 4-year degree in real estate. Attorneys are NOT exempt. FREC may allow 6 more months for physical hardship.

f: Continuing education — state the exact rule.
b:
14 hours per 2-year renewal period (after the first renewal): 3 hours Core Law + 3 hours Ethics and Business Practices + 8 hours specialty
Conditions: Applies to active and voluntary-inactive licensees.
Qualifications: Missing renewal → involuntary inactive (not void). Florida Bar members are exempt from CE.

f: First renewal timing — state the exact rule.
b:
18–24 months after initial licensure
Conditions: Later renewal periods are 24 months.

f: Reactivation from involuntary inactive — state the exact rule.
b:
≤12 months: 14 hours CE. More than 12 but less than 24 months: 28-hour reactivation course. More than 24 months: license expires (null and void).
Qualifications: Voluntary inactive can be renewed indefinitely with 14 hours CE per cycle.

f: Change of mailing or e-mail address — state the exact rule.
b: Notify DBPR in writing within 10 days

f: Reporting a crime (conviction, finding of guilt or plea) — state the exact rule.
b:
Within 30 days, in writing, including pleas of guilty or nolo contendere, to any crime in any jurisdiction
Conditions: Applies whether or not adjudication is withheld.

f: Broker license prerequisites — state the exact rule.
b:
24 months active sales associate license during the preceding 5 years; 72-hour broker course; broker exam
Conditions: Alternatives to the 24 months as a sales associate: salaried government employee holding a sales associate license, or broker licensed in another jurisdiction (same 24 months in 5 years). Sales associate post-licensing must be complete.

f: Broker post-license education — state the exact rule.
b:
60 hours (two 30-hour courses) before first broker renewal
Qualifications: Missing it voids the broker license.

f: FREC membership — state the exact rule.
b: 7 members: 4 brokers (active 5 preceding years), 1 broker or sales associate (active 2 preceding years), 2 consumer members (never licensed); at least 1 member 60 or older

f: FREC terms and quorum — state the exact rule.
b: 4-year terms; at most two consecutive terms (plus the rest of a predecessor's term); quorum 4 (51% of 7)

f: Duties: no brokerage relationship — state the exact rule.
b: 3 duties: deal honestly and fairly; disclose known facts materially affecting value of residential property not readily observable; account for all funds

f: Duties: transaction broker — state the exact rule.
b:
7 duties: the 3 above + use skill, care and diligence; present all offers and counteroffers timely (unless directed otherwise in writing); limited confidentiality (unless waived in writing); any additional duties mutually agreed
Qualifications: Not a fiduciary.

f: Duties: single agent — state the exact rule.
b:
9 duties: honesty/fairness; loyalty; confidentiality; obedience; full disclosure; accounting; skill, care and diligence; presenting offers; disclosing material facts
Conditions: Obedience covers lawful instructions only.
Qualifications: Florida prohibits single agency for both buyer and seller in the same transaction.

f: Residential sale (disclosure scope) — state the exact rule.
b:
Improved residential property of 4 units or fewer; unimproved residential property intended for 4 units or fewer; agricultural property of 10 acres or fewer
Qualifications: Not: commercial, leases/rentals (unless an option to buy ≤4 units), auctions, appraisals, business enterprises (except ≤4 residential units), open houses, casual encounters, general factual questions, parties already represented.

f: Designated sales associates — state the exact rule.
b:
Nonresidential transaction; buyer and seller each have assets of $1 million or more
Conditions: Requested in writing; disclosures signed.
Qualifications: Never in residential transactions.

f: Sales associate delivers deposit to broker — state the exact rule.
b: No later than the end of the next business day

f: Broker deposits escrow funds ('immediately') — state the exact rule.
b: No later than the end of the third business day after the brokerage receives the funds

f: Broker's own money in escrow — state the exact rule.
b:
Up to $1,000 in a sales escrow account; up to $5,000 in a property management escrow account
Qualifications: More than that = commingling.

f: Conflicting demands: notice to FREC — state the exact rule.
b:
Within 15 business days after the last demand (or after good-faith doubt arises)
Conditions: Only when the broker holds the funds.
Qualifications: Condo buyer cancels under s. 718.503; buyer's good-faith financing failure.

f: Conflicting demands: start a settlement procedure — state the exact rule.
b: Within 30 business days after the last demand

f: Mediation time limit — state the exact rule.
b: Must be completed within 90 days after the last demand; otherwise promptly use another procedure

f: Dispute settles before EDO issues — state the exact rule.
b: Notify FREC within 10 business days

f: Rental information for a fee: refunds — state the exact rule.
b:
Keep at most 25%: refund 75% if no rental is obtained; refund 100% if the information was not current or accurate
Qualifications: Violation: first-degree misdemeanor and license discipline. Older editions: demand within 30 days (not re-confirmed in the current text).

f: Record keeping — state the exact rule.
b: At least 5 years; if the records are involved in litigation, at least 2 years after the case and any appeal end (never less than 5 years in total)

f: Administrative fine — state the exact rule.
b: Up to $5,000 per violation (count)
Up to 10 years

f: Unlicensed practice — state the exact rule.
b: Third-degree felony (up to 5 years in prison and a $5,000 fine under the general sentencing statutes)

f: Appeal of a final order — state the exact rule.
b: Notice of appeal within 30 days after the final order, to the District Court of Appeal

f: Recovery Fund caps — state the exact rule.
b:
$50,000 per transaction (all claimants combined); $150,000 aggregate per licensee
Qualifications: No treble damages, court costs, attorney's fees or interest.

f: Fair housing protected classes — state the exact rule.
b: 1866: race (all property, no exceptions). 1968: race, color, religion, national origin. 1974: sex. 1988: familial status and handicap (disability).

f: Housing for older persons — state the exact rule.
b: 55+: at least 80% of occupied units have at least one person 55 or older (with published policies and age verification); or 62+: all occupants 62 or older

f: Fair housing exemptions — state the exact rule.
b:
Private owner of no more than 3 single-family homes selling/renting without a broker or discriminatory ads (one sale per 24 months if not the occupant); owner-occupied building of no more than 4 units ('Mrs. Murphy'); religious organizations and private clubs (members, non-commercial)
Conditions: Lost if a broker is used or a discriminatory ad is published.
Qualifications: Never for race (1866 Act).

f: Fair housing complaints — state the exact rule.
b: HUD complaint within 1 year; lawsuit within 2 years

f: Do Not Call established business relationship — state the exact rule.
b:
FCC rule: up to 18 months after a purchase/transaction; up to 3 months after an inquiry. FTC rule (since May 16, 2024): 540 days / 90 days.
Conditions: A specific request not to be called overrides it.
Qualifications: Written permission also allows calls.

f: CAN-SPAM opt-out — state the exact rule.
b:
Honored within 10 business days
Qualifications: Every commercial email needs a valid physical postal address.

f: TRID timing — state the exact rule.
b:
Loan Estimate within 3 business days after the application; Closing Disclosure received at least 3 business days before consummation (closing)
Qualifications: A corrected Closing Disclosure restarts the 3 days only if the APR becomes inaccurate, the loan product changes, or a prepayment penalty is added.

f: TILA right of rescission — state the exact rule.
b:
3 business days
Qualifications: Not for purchase-money loans or investment property.

f: Security deposit: notice of how held — state the exact rule.
b:
In the lease or within 30 days of receipt
Qualifications: Not required for landlords who rent fewer than 5 units.

f: Security deposit after move-out — state the exact rule.
b:
Return within 15 days if no claim; otherwise notice of claim within 30 days by certified mail (or by e-mail if both signed the e-mail addendum, since July 1, 2025); tenant has 15 days to object
Qualifications: Missing the 30-day notice forfeits the right to impose a claim.

f: Notice to end a tenancy without a specific term — state the exact rule.
b:
Year-to-year 60 days; quarter-to-quarter 30 days; month-to-month 30 days; week-to-week 7 days
Conditions: Written notice before the end of the period.
Qualifications: Manual and older books: month 15 days, quarter 45 days — outdated/incorrect (V-04).

f: Flood disclosure for residential leases — state the exact rule.
b:
At or before signing a residential lease of 1 year or longer
Qualifications: Leases shorter than 1 year are not covered. If the landlord fails to disclose and the tenant's belongings suffer a substantial flood loss, the tenant may terminate within 30 days after the damage.

f: Homestead size (creditor protection) — state the exact rule.
b:
1/2 acre of contiguous land within a municipality; 160 contiguous acres outside a municipality
Qualifications: No protection against property taxes and assessments, debts for purchase, improvement or repair, or labor on the property.

f: Condominium cancellation rights — state the exact rule.
b:
Developer sale: 15 days. Resale: 7 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays, after signing and receiving the documents (since July 1, 2025; older books: 3 business days).
Conditions: Both rights end at closing.

f: Timeshare cancellation — state the exact rule.
b: Until midnight of the 10th calendar day after the later of signing or receiving the last required document; cannot be waived

f: HOA disclosure summary — state the exact rule.
b:
Buyer may void the contract within 3 days after receiving the summary or before closing, whichever occurs first
Qualifications: Not waivable; ends at closing. Not for condominiums, co-ops or timeshares.

f: Adverse possession (Florida) — state the exact rule.
b: 7 years of continuous possession, either under color of title (recorded written instrument) or without color of title if the possessor pays the taxes within 1 year of entering and files a return with the property appraiser within 30 days after paying

f: Easement by prescription (Florida) — state the exact rule.
b: 20 years of open, continuous, adverse use

f: Deed witnesses — state the exact rule.
b:
Grantor signs in the presence of 2 witnesses
Conditions: Notary acknowledgment needed for recording, not validity.
Qualifications: Leases: no witnesses required (V-05).
6 miles × 6 miles = 36 square miles = 36 sections
1 mile × 1 mile = 1 square mile = 640 acres
43,560 square feet
5,280 feet

f: Square yard — state the exact rule.
b: 9 square feet (3 ft × 3 ft)

f: Florida principal meridian and base line — state the exact rule.
b: Intersect in Tallahassee

f: Statute of limitations (Florida) — state the exact rule.
b: Written contract: 5 years. Oral contract: 4 years.

f: Statute of frauds — state the exact rule.
b:
Contracts for the sale of real property, and contracts not performable within 1 year, must be in writing and signed by the party to be charged
Qualifications: Leases of 1 year or less may be oral.

f: Written listing agreement rules — state the exact rule.
b: Definite expiration date; property description, price and terms, fee, principal's signature; no clause requiring the seller to give notice to cancel after expiration (no automatic renewal); copy to the person signing within 24 hours

f: Lead-based paint — state the exact rule.
b:
Housing built before 1978: disclose known lead paint and hazards, give the EPA pamphlet; buyers get a 10-day inspection opportunity (may be waived or changed in writing)
Qualifications: Tenants get the disclosure but not the 10-day period.

f: Satisfaction of mortgage — state the exact rule.
b: Lender records within 60 days of full payment

f: Florida usury — state the exact rule.
b: 18% per year simple interest on loans of $500,000 or less; 25% on larger loans. Criminal usury: over 25% up to 45% = misdemeanor; over 45% = felony.

f: Qualifying ratios (course convention) — state the exact rule.
b:
Conventional 28% housing / 36% total; FHA 31% / 43%
Conditions: Teaching benchmarks, not statutes.

f: PMI trigger (conventional) — state the exact rule.
b: Required when LTV is above 80%

f: FHA minimum down payment — state the exact rule.
b: 3.5% (with qualifying credit)

f: Discount point — state the exact rule.
b:
1 point = 1% of the loan amount; each point raises the lender's yield by about 1/8%
Conditions: 1/8% is a rule of thumb used in the course.

f: Reverse mortgage age — state the exact rule.
b: 62 or older

f: Documentary stamp tax on deeds — state the exact rule.
b: $0.70 per $100 or portion thereof of total consideration (round UP to the next $100); Miami-Dade: $0.60 per $100 for single-family residences, other property $0.60 + $0.45 surtax

f: Documentary stamp tax on notes — state the exact rule.
b: $0.35 per $100 or portion thereof

f: Nonrecurring intangible tax — state the exact rule.
b:
2 mills (0.002) × the amount of the NEW mortgage; no rounding
Qualifications: Not due again on an assumed mortgage when it was paid originally and the debt is unchanged (s. 199.145(3), V-25).

f: Proration conventions (Florida course) — state the exact rule.
b:
365-day year (actual days in each month); the buyer is responsible for the day of closing
Conditions: Follow the question if it states another method. No statute or rule sets these; they come from the contract and the course.

f: Homestead tax exemptions — state the exact rule.
b:
First $25,000 of assessed value: all taxes. Additional up to $25,000 (CPI-indexed since 2025: $25,722 for 2025) on assessed value above $50,000: non-school taxes only.
Conditions: Must own and occupy as permanent residence on January 1.

f: Widow/widower, blind, totally and permanently disabled exemption — state the exact rule.
b:
$5,000
Conditions: Florida resident.
Qualifications: Older books: $500.

f: Save Our Homes cap — state the exact rule.
b:
Assessed value of a homestead rises no more than 3% per year or the CPI change, whichever is less; portability: up to $500,000 of the benefit moves to a new Florida homestead established within 3 years
Qualifications: Resets to just value on change of ownership. November 2026 ballot measure may change it from 2027 (V-23).

f: Property tax calendar — state the exact rule.
b: Assessment date January 1; TRIM notice within 55 days after certification (usually August); due November 1 with discounts of 4% (Nov), 3% (Dec), 2% (Jan), 1% (Feb); delinquent April 1 (or 60 days after the bill was mailed, if later)
1 mill = $1 per $1,000 of taxable value = 0.001

f: Depreciation (cost recovery) — state the exact rule.
b: Residential rental: 27.5 years. Nonresidential: 39 years. Land never depreciates.

f: Principal residence gain exclusion — state the exact rule.
b:
$250,000 single; $500,000 married filing jointly; owned and used as main home 2 of the last 5 years
Conditions: Generally not available if the exclusion was used on another home sold within the previous 2 years.
Laws passed by the Florida Legislature, organized by chapter and section (e.g., s. 475.25).
Florida's real estate license law: brokers, sales associates, schools, appraisers (Part II).
General law for all professions regulated by the DBPR (applications, investigations, discipline procedures).

Rules adopted by state agencies under authority given by a statute. FREC's rules are Chapter 61J2.
Note: A rule has the force of law but must stay within its statute.
The FREC's rule chapter in the Florida Administrative Code (escrow, advertising, education, offices).

Law made by court decisions that interpret statutes or develop common law; e.g., Johnson v. Davis (seller must disclose known latent defects).
Note: Florida (like most of the US) is a common-law system; Portugal is a civil-law system.
Legal rules developed by courts over time, rather than written in a code.
Florida Real Estate Commission: 7 members appointed by the Governor; makes rules and disciplines licensees.
Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation; its Division of Real Estate provides FREC's administrative services, issues licenses and investigates complaints.
Land plus everything permanently attached to it (improvements), and the rights that go with ownership.
Real estate together with the bundle of legal rights of ownership.
Movable items not attached to land (chattels); co-op shares are personal property.

A registered trademark identifying members of the National Association of REALTORS® (NAR), who agree to its Code of Ethics.
Note: Not a license. A licensee need not be a REALTOR®.
National Association of REALTORS®, the largest US trade association for real estate professionals.
Member of the National Association of Real Estate Brokers (NAREB).
Specialty of managing property for owners: leasing, rent collection, maintenance.
Property with a unique use, such as churches, schools, hospitals.

Person licensed to perform real estate services for compensation, but only under the direction of an employing broker or owner-developer.
Note: Florida term for what other states call a salesperson.
Person licensed to perform real estate services for others for compensation in their own name; may open an office and hold escrow.
A person with a broker license who chooses to work under another broker.
Anything of value — money, gifts, property — paid or promised, or even expected, for a real estate service.

Person authorized by a power of attorney to sign for another; exempt only for executing contracts or conveyances.
Note: Not the same as an attorney at law (lawyer).
Plea of 'no contest': the defendant does not admit guilt but accepts the penalty. Must be reported within 30 days like a guilty plea.

Agreement letting nonresident licensees of certain states obtain a Florida license by passing a 40-question Florida law exam.
Note: Not 'reciprocity' — the exam uses the precise term.
Rule-making power exercised by an agency (FREC adopting 61J2 rules).
Power of an agency to decide disputes and impose discipline (FREC final orders).
Recording a licensee's name, address, employer and status in DBPR records.
DBPR's certification that a person has met the qualifications to hold a license.
Registration allowing a sales associate to work for several connected entities of one owner-developer.

Separate licenses a BROKER may hold for separate, unconnected brokerages.
Note: Sales associates cannot hold multiple licenses.
License whose holder is registered with an employing broker (or, for a broker, an office) and may practice.
Status chosen by the licensee; may be renewed indefinitely with CE.
Status caused by failure to renew; expires (void) after 2 years.
The license has ceased to exist; the person must requalify.
A license that exists but cannot be used, e.g., a sales associate with no employing broker.
45-hour course a sales associate must complete before the first renewal.
14 hours every 2-year renewal period after the first: 3 Core Law + 3 Ethics and Business Practices + 8 specialty.
A licensee providing limited representation to a buyer, seller or both; not a fiduciary. Presumed in Florida.
A broker who represents one party (the principal) as a fiduciary.
A licensee works with a party without representing them; owes 3 duties.
Acting as fiduciary agent for both buyer and seller in one transaction; prohibited in Florida.
A person in a relationship of trust who must put the principal's interests first.
The person a single agent represents.
A party a licensee works with but does not represent as a fiduciary.
Transaction-broker duty not to reveal that the seller will accept less, the buyer will pay more, a party's motivation, or other information a party asks to keep confidential.
Signed consent of a principal allowing the single agent to become a transaction broker.
Sale of ≤4 residential units, unimproved land for ≤4 units, or agricultural property ≤10 acres.
A fact that would affect a reasonable person's decision or the property's value.
A hidden defect not discoverable by ordinary inspection.
Associate appointed as single agent for one party in a nonresidential deal where each party has $1M+ in assets.
Account holding money belonging to others (deposits, rents).

Deposit a buyer gives to show good faith, usually held in escrow.
Note: Not the Portuguese 'sinal' — no automatic double-return rule.
Mixing personal or business funds with escrow funds.
Using escrow funds for personal or unauthorized purposes.
Order from FREC deciding who receives disputed escrow funds held by a broker.
Lawsuit in which the broker deposits disputed funds with the court and asks it to decide who is entitled.
Non-binding process with a neutral third party; requires all parties' written consent.
Binding decision by a neutral arbitrator; requires all parties' consent.
Advertisement that fails to include the brokerage's registered name.
Payment for referring business; restricted by Chapter 475 and prohibited by RESPA in most residential financed deals.
Competitors agreeing on commission rates; illegal under antitrust law.
Additional location where the broker conducts business; must be registered.
A complaint alleging facts that, if true, would violate a statute or rule.
Panel that decides whether the investigation supports filing a formal complaint.
Judge from the Division of Administrative Hearings who conducts formal hearings and recommends an order.
FREC's decision on discipline.
Fixed fine for a listed minor violation, offered instead of formal proceedings.
Written notice for a first minor violation, letting the licensee correct it.
Reckless indifference to others' rights — more than simple carelessness.
False statement or concealment of a material fact.
State fund that pays consumers who cannot collect a judgment against a licensee arising from a brokerage transaction.
Directing buyers or renters toward or away from areas based on a protected class.
Inducing owners to sell by suggesting a protected class is moving in.
A lender refusing loans or changing terms in certain areas for discriminatory reasons.
Households with children under 18, pregnant women, or people obtaining custody.
Physical change to a unit for a person with a disability, generally at the tenant's expense.
Change in rules or policies for a person with a disability (e.g., assistance animal despite a no-pets rule).
Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act: closing disclosures and anti-kickback rules for federally related residential loans.
Truth in Lending Act: disclosure of credit costs, APR, advertising trigger terms, right of rescission.
Annual percentage rate: the yearly cost of credit including interest and certain fees.
Specific credit term in an ad (down payment amount, payment amount, number of payments, finance charge) that requires full disclosure.
TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure rule: Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure.

Equal Credit Opportunity Act: no credit discrimination by race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age (if able to contract), public assistance income, or good-faith exercise of consumer credit rights.
Americans with Disabilities Act: accessibility of public accommodations and commercial facilities.
Home Mortgage Disclosure Act: lenders report lending data that reveals patterns like redlining.
Ownership rights: possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, disposition.
Ownership of indeterminate duration (fee simple, life estate).
The most complete ownership, inheritable and unconditional.
Ownership that can be lost if a stated condition occurs or is breached.

Ownership limited to the life of a person.
Note: Similar in purpose to usufruto, but a distinct legal form.
Life estate measured by the life of someone other than the life tenant.
Future interest passing to a third party when a life estate ends.
Future interest returning to the grantor (or heirs) when a life estate ends.
Damage or neglect by a life tenant that harms the future interest.
Right of possession under a lease, without ownership.
Lease for a fixed term (any length); ends without notice.
Lease renewing period to period (week, month, quarter, year) until notice.
Tenancy of indefinite duration terminable by proper notice.
Holdover tenant who stays without the landlord's consent.
Tenant pays fixed rent; landlord pays operating expenses.
Tenant pays rent plus some or all property expenses (triple net: taxes, insurance, maintenance).
Rent includes a percentage of the tenant's gross sales, usually above a base rent.
Long-term lease of land on which the tenant builds.
Transfer of the ENTIRE remaining lease term.
Transfer of part of the remaining term or part of the space.
Co-ownership with undivided, possibly unequal shares and no survivorship.

f: Define: Joint tenancy with right of survivorship
b: Co-ownership with the four unities; deceased owner's share passes to survivors.
Ownership by a married couple as one unit; survivorship; protected from one spouse's creditors.
Possession, Interest, Time, Title.
Court action to divide co-owned property or force its sale.
A Florida owner's primary residence, with creditor protection, transfer restrictions, and tax exemption.
Ownership of a unit in fee simple plus an undivided share of common elements, created by a recorded declaration.
Parts of a condominium owned in common (lobby, pool, roof).
A corporation owns the building; residents own shares and hold proprietary leases (personal property).
Lease giving a co-op shareholder the right to occupy a unit.
Right to use a unit for a set period each year.
Homeowners' association: mandatory-membership community governed by recorded covenants.
Community Development District: special-purpose local government that finances community infrastructure through assessments.
Ownership and the evidence of it.
Property passing to the state when an owner dies without a will or heirs.
Government's power to take private property for public use with just compensation (condemnation).
Acquiring title by open, notorious, hostile, continuous possession for 7 years in Florida plus color of title or payment of taxes.
A document that appears to give title but is defective.
Dying with / without a valid will.
Gift of real property by will / its recipient.
Transfer of an intestate's property to heirs under statute.
The person conveying / receiving title by deed.
Grantor warrants title against defects from any time.
Grantor warrants only against defects arising during their ownership.
Implies the grantor owns the property but gives no warranties.
Conveys whatever interest the grantor has, with no warranties.
A claim or defect that impairs title.
Formal declaration before a notary that the signer signed voluntarily; needed to record.
Covenant that the grantor owns the property and has the right to convey it.
Notice the law presumes from public records or visible possession.
What a person actually knows.
Summary of all recorded documents affecting a property's title.
Policy protecting against losses from title defects existing before the policy date.
Any claim or limitation on title (lien, easement, restriction, encroachment).
A claim against property as security for a debt.
Lien on one property (mortgage, property tax, construction lien).
Lien on all the debtor's property (judgment, IRS lien).
A lienholder agreeing to a lower priority.
Easement benefiting an adjoining parcel (dominant) over a burdened parcel (servient); runs with the land.
Easement benefiting a person or company (e.g., utility), not a parcel.
Easement acquired by 20 years of open, continuous, adverse use in Florida.

Revocable personal permission to use land; not an interest in land.
Note: Different meaning from a real estate license.
A structure or improvement extending onto another's land.
Private limitation on use recorded in a deed or plat.
Personal property attached to real property so that it becomes part of it.
Item a business tenant installs for its trade; remains the tenant's personal property.
Annual crops produced by labor; personal property.
Rights of owners along rivers and streams.
Rights of owners along oceans, seas and large lakes.
Gradual addition of land by water deposits (owner gains) / sudden loss or change (boundary does not move).
Description using a point of beginning, directions (courses) and distances, returning to the POB.
Starting and ending point of a metes-and-bounds description.
Description by lot and block numbers on a recorded plat.
Recorded map of a subdivision.
System of townships and sections measured from principal meridians and base lines.
6 × 6 mile square, 36 sections.
1 square mile, 640 acres.
A foot of frontage along a street or water; the first dimension given.
Promise for a promise (e.g., sale contract).
Promise for an act (e.g., option, reward).
Obligations still to perform / fully performed.
No contract at all / one party may cancel / valid but courts won't enforce.
Law requiring certain contracts (sale of real estate, >1 year) to be written and signed.
Something of value exchanged; mutual promises suffice.
A response that changes the terms; it rejects and terminates the original offer.
Contract giving the optionee the right to buy at set terms during a period; optionor is bound.
Buyer's interest under a signed sale contract before closing.
Court order to perform the contract as agreed.
Damages agreed in advance (often the deposit).
The broker whose efforts started an uninterrupted chain of events leading to the sale.
Listing given to several brokers; only the procuring broker is paid; owner may sell free.
One brokerage; owner keeps the right to sell without commission.
One brokerage earns the commission no matter who sells.
Broker keeps any amount above the seller's net price.
Date the last party signs or initials the final offer/counteroffer and it is communicated; contract deadlines run from it.

f: Define: Time is of the essence
b: Clause making contract deadlines strict.
Seller makes no repairs; buyer may inspect and cancel within the inspection period.
The borrower's written promise to repay the debt.

Security instrument pledging property for a debt.
Note: In US usage 'mortgage' is the document, not the loan.
Borrower (gives the mortgage) / lender (receives it).
The borrower keeps title; the lender holds a lien (Florida).
Lets the lender demand the entire balance on default.
Balance becomes due if the property is transferred.
The mortgage is defeated (cancelled) when the debt is paid.
Borrower not personally liable; lender looks only to the property.
Buyer takes over the loan and becomes personally liable.
Substitution of a new party that releases the original borrower.
Buyer takes title and pays the loan without personal liability.
Borrower's right to pay off the debt and stop foreclosure until the sale.
Judgment for the unpaid balance after a foreclosure sale.
Sale where the lender accepts less than the amount owed.

f: Define: Deed in lieu of foreclosure
b: Borrower deeds the property to the lender to avoid foreclosure; junior liens survive.
Principal, interest, taxes, insurance — the monthly housing payment.
Charging interest above the legal maximum.
Loan-to-value ratio: loan ÷ lesser of price or appraised value.
Federal Housing Administration (HUD): insures loans; borrower pays MIP.
Department of Veterans Affairs: guarantees loans to eligible veterans.
Private mortgage insurance on conventional loans above 80% LTV.
Level payments covering interest and principal until fully repaid.
Large final payment on a partially amortized loan.
Adjustable-rate mortgage: rate = index + margin, limited by caps.
Covers real and personal property.
Covers several parcels; release clause frees parcels as paid.
New junior loan that includes an existing loan.
Seller finances part of the price.
Lender pays an owner aged 62+; repaid on sale, move-out or death.
Lenders who originate loans.
Buyers of existing loans (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Ginnie Mae guarantees).
Depositors withdrawing funds for higher yields elsewhere, reducing mortgage money.
Prepaid interest: 1 point = 1% of the loan.
Dividing an expense or income between buyer and seller as of closing.
Paid at the end of the period (Florida property taxes, mortgage interest).
Paid at the start of the period (rent, insurance premiums).
An amount a party owes at closing.
An amount a party receives at closing.
Florida excise tax on deeds ($0.70/$100) and notes ($0.35/$100).
Florida one-time tax of 2 mills on new mortgages.
Comparative market analysis by a licensee to suggest a price range.
Broker price opinion, often for lenders; chargeable but not an appraisal.
Most probable price in an arm's-length sale between informed parties under no unusual pressure.
Legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, maximally productive use.
A buyer won't pay more than the cost of an equally desirable substitute.
Value increase from combining parcels / the act of combining them.
Weighing the approaches to reach a final value estimate (not averaging).
Cost of an exact replica.
Cost of a building with equal utility using current materials.
Loss from outdated design or features.
Loss from factors outside the property; always incurable.
Net operating income: effective gross income minus operating expenses.
NOI ÷ value.
Gross rent multiplier (price ÷ monthly rent) / gross income multiplier (price ÷ annual income).
Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice.
Using borrowed money to increase return on equity.
NOI minus debt service.
Selling a business (goodwill, inventory, fixtures, possibly real estate).
Intangible value of a business's reputation and customer base.
According to value.
Florida's term for market value used by the property appraiser.
Truth in Millage notice showing proposed assessments and rates (August).
County board that hears property assessment appeals.
Lien sold to an investor to collect delinquent property taxes.
Charge on properties specially benefited by a public improvement.
Tax rate in mills (1 mill = $1 per $1,000 of taxable value).
Cap on annual homestead assessment increases (3% or CPI, whichever is less).
Cost of property / cost plus improvements minus depreciation.
Tax-deferred exchange of like-kind investment or business real property.
Non-like-kind value received in an exchange; taxable to the extent of gain.
Seller receives payments over time and reports gain as received.
Government power to regulate for health, safety and welfare; no compensation owed.
Owner's lawsuit claiming a regulation amounts to a taking.
Local government's long-range land-use plan; zoning implements it.
Permission to deviate from a dimensional rule because of hardship unique to the parcel.
Use allowed in a zone with case-by-case approval.
Lawful use that predates current zoning ('grandfathered').
Planned unit development mixing uses with clustered density and open space.
Document allowing a building to be occupied after final inspection.
Federal law imposing strict, joint and several liability for cleaning up contaminated sites.
Abandoned or underused contaminated site being redeveloped.
Naturally occurring radioactive gas; Florida requires a disclosure in sale and lease contracts.

f: A licensed Florida brokerage hires an unlicensed assistant and pays $150 for every buyer she shows a home to. Lawful?
b: No. Showing property for compensation per transaction is a real estate service for another for compensation; she needs a license. A salary for clerical work only would be lawful.

f: Who issues a Florida real estate license, and who may revoke it?
b: The DBPR issues it; the FREC may revoke it (after due process).

f: A licensee misses the 45-hour post-license course before the first renewal. Result?
b: The license becomes null and void; to practice again they must requalify from the 63-hour course and exam.

f: A Florida broker acts as single agent for a seller and wants to work with a buyer on the same property. What is required?
b: The seller's written consent to transition to transaction broker before the change; the broker then acts as transaction broker for both parties.

f: Which three requirements apply to every written listing in Florida?
b: A definite expiration date; no automatic renewal clause; a copy delivered to the person signing within 24 hours.

f: May a Florida sales associate sue the buyer directly for an unpaid commission?
b: No. The associate's claim is against the employing broker; only the broker can sue the party who owes the brokerage fee.

f: The buyer defaults on a Florida contract. Does the seller receive double the deposit?
b: No. The seller's remedy depends on the contract (often the deposit as liquidated damages). The broker releases escrowed funds only per the contract, written agreement, or a settlement procedure.

f: What does a buyer hold between contract and closing?
b: Equitable title.

f: Who customarily pays deed stamps in Florida, and on what amount?
b: The seller, on the full purchase price (including any mortgage assumed), at $0.70 per $100 or portion.

f: Why can a homestead's school taxable value be higher than its non-school taxable value?
b: The additional homestead exemption applies only to non-school levies.

f: Is recording required for a Florida deed to be valid between grantor and grantee?
b: No. Delivery and acceptance make it valid; recording gives constructive notice to the world.

f: Which deed best cures a cloud on title?
b: A quitclaim deed.

f: A married couple takes title 'John and Mary Smith, husband and wife'. John dies. Who owns the property?
b: Mary, automatically, by survivorship under tenancy by the entireties.

f: Which buyer owns real property: the condo buyer or the co-op buyer?
b: The condo buyer.

f: A life tenant leases the property for 10 years and dies after 2. What happens to the lease?
b: It ends at the life tenant's death; the life tenant could only convey what she had.

f: Which creditor can force the sale of a Florida homestead: a credit-card judgment creditor or the county for unpaid property taxes?
b: The county for unpaid property taxes.

f: How many acres is a 435,600 sq ft parcel?
Which income figure do qualifying ratios use?
b: Gross monthly income.

f: Does a deed in lieu of foreclosure wipe out a second mortgage?
b: No. The lender takes title subject to junior liens; only foreclosure can eliminate them.

f: A landlord with a 4-unit building who lives in one unit refuses to rent to a family with children and uses no broker or ads. Which exemption might apply?
b: The 'Mrs. Murphy' owner-occupied (≤4 units) exemption under the federal FHA — but never for race, and lost if a broker or discriminatory ad is used.

f: Does a sales associate's personal Facebook ad for a listing need the brokerage name?
b: Yes.

f: How much notice ends a quarter-to-quarter tenancy without a specific term?
b: At least 30 days before the end of the quarter.

f: Is a Florida seller required to obtain an energy rating of the home before listing?
b: No. The requirement is to give the buyer the energy-efficiency rating information at or before contract.
